html:
If reading or watching the news feels less like staying informed and more like a daily horror or heartbreak, you’re not alone. Many of us are carrying a kind of civic homesickness. It’s what happens when the truths we presumed were universal start to crumble. Sometimes, differences of worldview so profound have emerged that even dinner conversations feel like foreign policy negotiations.

How do we give shape to this disquiet? We might call it fatigue, burnout, or ‘just needing a break from the world’, but often it’s grief – mourning for a faith we once had in fellow citizens to recognise a certain decency or sense of fairness. It isn’t partisan; it’s human, and it has a name. Civic grief doesn’t care which side of the table you sit on. It can visit anyone who has seen their values of citizenship and belonging abandoned or even opposed by their neighbours or friends or country.

If this sounds familiar, take heart. The ache itself is proof of care, a sign that some part of you still believes we can do better. Around the world, survey after survey shows people losing faith in institutions, leaders, and even each other. Freedom House’s 2026 report found that global freedom declined for the 20th consecutive year in 2025, with political rights and civil liberties deteriorating in 54 countries and improving in only 35. Those numbers have lived counterparts: military coups, efforts to weaken constitutional safeguards, violence against peaceful protesters, attacks on courts and journalists, and families increasingly unable to discuss public life without treating one another as hostile witnesses. The grief, in other words, is not floating above reality. It is responding to it. In naming civic grief for what it is, we can find a more honest place to begin, and perhaps a way to see what is still in common even across bitter divides. First, civic grief needs to be understood more clearly.

The first stage is denial, a most civilised coping mechanism. It wears a suit, reads editorials, and insists that things are not as bad as they look. We might remind ourselves that democratic government has survived worse: wars, recessions, demagogues, corruption. We use history like a sedative, and call the system ‘resilient’, confident the pendulum will swing back. We vote and try to convince ourselves that the institutions are working as they should. Denial has its uses, but slowly we begin to absorb the scope of the crisis in small, unavoidable doses.

The trouble comes when denial hardens into complacency. In places where the erosion of our civic life is subtle, it is easy to believe that real breakdowns aren’t a crisis. If we decide events are a ‘temporary disturbance’, nothing fundamental has to change. Scaled up, it turns into a false, reassuring voice saying ‘institutions are basically fine’ long after the evidence disagrees.

The cycle of scandals, polarisation and moral fatigue accumulates until they register as the new reality

When denial cracks, anger usually walks in, puts its feet on the table, and opens a social media account. Biologically, it is the nervous system in fight or flight. The amygdala turns up the volume on threat, stress hormones spike, and attention narrows to villains and blame. It can fix on corrupt officials, apathetic neighbours, ‘elites’ or ‘the media’. In one country, it centres on police violence or election fraud; in another, on inequality or culture wars. It often shows up as indignation at bias, apathy or the endless loop of shouting heads who look like they are debating but are mostly performing disbelief, showing they still care enough to be furious. Algorithms love this, which is why anger is the grief stage most compatible with modern technology. We mistake outrage for engagement, and forget that noise and signal are not the same. Yet anger has a purpose. It is the immune response of conscience. The task is to keep it from turning autoimmune, and to let it fuel stewardship instead of scorched earth.

The next stage of civic grief is bargaining. It sets in once the adrenaline cools. This is the ‘if-then’ logic of the optimist feeling despair. If we educate the next generation better, if more people vote, if we just talk across the aisle, things will get better. Bargaining is democracy’s prayer: let us return to normalcy, and we promise to behave better this time. It is noble but delusional, for it assumes the old ‘normal’ can be restored. Still, bargaining reveals something precious: the refusal to give up. Even naive hope has moral worth. Bargaining may not save democracy, but it prevents cynicism from claiming the soul entirely.

The fourth stage of civic grief is depression, the weight of disillusionment. The cycle of scandals, polarisation and moral fatigue accumulates until they register as the new reality. This is the stage of numbness: when people withdraw from the public sphere not out of apathy, but out of emotional self-preservation. The ballot box feels like theatre. Debate feels like déjà vu. Facts feel negotiable. Philosophically, this is a dangerous moment, when the demos, the people, cease to believe their will matters. This is a kind of soft despotism from long ago: not tyranny of chains, but of indifference. Depression acknowledges that idealism has limits. Here is when people often ask, what if the system is functioning exactly as designed? What if the system is no longer democratic?

Accepting the stages of our civic grief is important and does not mean surrender. It means we can move on to seeing more clearly. It is where citizens begin to understand that democracy was never an inheritance, but an ongoing responsibility and an act of stewardship and creation. Acceptance is where we stop waiting for ‘the adults in the room’ to fix things and recognise that we are the adults. The work of democracy, it turns out, is not glamorous: it’s reading city budgets, attending community meetings, and listening to people who annoy us. It also requires humility. The idea that one political side or ideology can ‘save’ democracy misunderstands it. Democracy, by nature, is a tense structure built to hold disagreement without collapse. The goal was never unanimity, but coexistence. Democracy was never meant to eliminate conflict. It was meant to civilise it, to keep disagreement from becoming dehumanisation, and to turn competing claims into conditions where dignity, security, opportunity, collective wellbeing and belonging remain possible.

Coming through to the other side of civic grief means no more nostalgia for the previous order. Instead, it brings us to reinvention and action. This kind of hope insists that, even when institutions falter, individuals must act to represent democracy and can still support democratic values of curiosity, empathy, courage, restraint. Hope becomes real when it stops being a feeling and becomes a discipline. It means choosing one part of the common life and tending it close to the ground: a school, a library, a neighbourhood association, a local campaign, a food pantry, a veterans’ organisation, an environmental group. Democracy is rebuilt there, through habits that may outlast us: transparency where suspicion could take root, listening where contempt would be easier, and enough restraint to remember that opponents are still people, not symbols arranged for our convenience.

Emotions are not irrational storms; they are intelligence about what we value. Civic grief says that fairness, dignity and shared obligation were precious enough that their loss hurts. In the body, it feels like heaviness or fatigue. In the mind, it becomes questions: who are we if what we were told to trust keeps failing us? What does it mean to be a ‘good citizen’ when the rules feel soft for some and razor sharp for others? How do you keep caring about an ‘us’ that no longer feels shared?

It can be unsettling to realise that the person who seems to live on the other side of every issue may be grieving a different story about what was lost, but they still felt something crack where they thought ‘we’ lived. Calling this civic grief does not erase our differences; it gives us a shared language for the ache and a first step toward something more useful than fighting or shutting down.
